forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.mechanism: The Niger compiler states that assisted natural regeneration, by improving vegetation cover and increasing woody production, helps reduce the impacts of long droughts during the rainy season [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_2325_2017_drought_impacts].
forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state an effect: a single practitioner rating from a Niger technology sheet, with no measured drought outcome [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_2325_2017_drought_impacts]. Any effect would be off-site for farmers, arriving downstream or at landscape scale rather than on their plots. What is missing is a second independent source or one measured finding.

forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.mechanism: The Niger compiler reports that by improving vegetation cover and increasing woody production, assisted natural regeneration helps reduce the impacts of long droughts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_2325_2017_drought_impacts].
forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state an effect: a single compiler rating from Niger, with no measured drought outcome [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_2325_2017_drought_impacts]. Any effect would be off-site for farmers, arriving downstream or at landscape scale rather than on their plots. What is missing is a second independent source or one measured finding.

forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.mechanism: Compilers for assisted natural regeneration in Niger and Bangladesh rate soil loss and surface runoff as moderately reduced, which is how this row reaches flood [ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_1626_2014_soil_loss, ev_runoff_reduction_wocat_4372_2019_surface_runoff].
forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.conditionality: No unit rates or measures downstream flooding directly; the link runs only through runoff and erosion proxies. All units are practitioner ratings from technology sheets.

forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.mechanism: WOCAT compilers in Niger rate assisted natural regeneration as increasing crop, fodder and livestock production: in the agro-pastoral zone it raised millet and sorghum production in fields, and vegetation cover on sylvo-pastoral land increased by more than 100%, lifting fodder supply [ev_crop_yield_wocat_2325_2017_crop_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_2325_2017_fodder_production, ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_2325_2017_animal_production, ev_crop_yield_wocat_1626_2014_crop_production].
forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.conditionality: All units are compiler ratings from Niger, with no measured yields or comparison plots, and fodder enters as a component proxy for the production gap.

forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.mechanism: Recurrent costs are the annual maintenance entered by WOCAT compilers for assisted natural regeneration in Niger (US$108/ha per year) and Bangladesh (US$339.29/ha per year) [ev_project_cost_wocat_2325_2017_maintenance, ev_project_cost_wocat_4372_2019_maintenance].
forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.conditionality: Both values are converted by compilers from local-currency entries and come from just a pair of technology sheets.

forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.mechanism: WOCAT compilers rate the long-term returns of assisted natural regeneration as positive or very positive in Niger and Bangladesh, and in Niger report that it contributes to food security and self-sufficiency in the southern regions and lowers the risk of production failure [ev_economic_return_wocat_2325_2017_costbenefit_establishment_long, ev_economic_return_wocat_4372_2019_costbenefit_establishment_long, ev_food_security_wocat_2325_2017_food_security_selfsufficiency, ev_food_security_wocat_1626_2014_risk_of_production_failure].
forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.conditionality: Every unit is a compiler rating; returns and food security are proxies for poverty, and no unit measures household income or poverty outcomes.

forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.mechanism: WOCAT compilers in Niger and Bangladesh rate assisted natural regeneration as reducing surface runoff and soil loss, and the Bangladesh sheet also rates downstream siltation as reduced [ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_1626_2014_soil_loss, ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_4372_2019_soil_loss, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_4372_2019_downstream_siltation].
forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.conditionality: All units are compiler ratings, with runoff and siltation entering as components; no unit measures soil loss.

forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.mechanism: The Bangladesh compiler rates assisted natural regeneration as slightly decreasing downstream siltation, the sediment pathway to water quality [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_4372_2019_downstream_siltation].
forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state an effect: a single compiler rating, and siltation is only a component of water quality [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_4372_2019_downstream_siltation]. Any effect would be off-site for farmers, arriving downstream or at landscape scale rather than on their plots. What is missing is a second independent source or one measured finding.

forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.mechanism: The Niger compiler rates assisted natural regeneration as slightly improving water harvesting and collection [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1626_2014_harvesting_collection_of_water].
forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state an effect: a single compiler rating without a measured water outcome or a stated mechanism [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1626_2014_harvesting_collection_of_water]. Any effect would be off-site for farmers, arriving downstream or at landscape scale rather than on their plots. What is missing is a second independent source or one measured finding.

forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.mechanism: The Niger compiler rates assisted natural regeneration as lowering wind velocity, a shelter effect of regenerated woody cover [ev_windbreak_protection_wocat_1626_2014_wind_velocity].
forest_restoration__assisted_regeneratio.conditionality: This is a single practitioner rating of everyday wind speed, not of cyclone or storm damage.

forest_restoration__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: Putting tree cover back on cleared or degraded land rebuilds the structure that forest species need, and then lets dispersers do the rest. Measured against degraded ecosystems across 221 study landscapes worldwide, forest restoration enhanced biodiversity by 15-84% and vegetation structure by 36-77% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles16_1]. How the cover is re-established changes the result: natural regeneration surpassed active restoration for plants, birds and invertebrates, with restoration success 34 to 56% higher after controlling for forest cover, precipitation and time [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles17_1]. Recovery is a function of time since disturbance [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_1], and the clock is slow — a secondary Atlantic forest was estimated to need 65 years, with a range of 23 to 178, to reach a proportion of 80% animal-dispersed species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_2]. What accelerates it is anything that brings seed in or keeps grazing out: beneath framework-species plantings, tree seedlings of many species recruited, 25 of them animal-dispersed and 11 wind-dispersed [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wydhayagarn09_1]; artificial perches brought native zoochoric regeneration that was absent from the planted rings [ev_biodiversity_outcome_loureiro21_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_loureiro21_2]; and Senegalese exclosures carried 27 woody species after a year against 51 in the 5- and 12-year enclosures, more than 52% higher richness [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1]. Practitioners implementing these technologies in Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Ethiopia, India, Niger and Turkmenistan record plant, animal and habitat diversity rising as cover returns and protection holds [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_7460_2024_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_7460_2024_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_4372_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_5243_2019_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_2325_2017_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1529_2012_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1414_2011_animal_diversity]. The other route is keeping the forest that exists, since the governance instruments that retain cover also hold the habitat: GEF sustainable forest management sites lost about 0.27% less forest each year than matched areas [ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_1], community forest management in Nepal reduced deforestation [ev_landscape_forest_cover_iufro20_1], payments improved forest cover and reduced deforestation in pooled analysis [ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_2], and participatory management is credited with regeneration of degraded forests and protection of biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_ieg13_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_2]. A global analysis of community forests found environmental condition improved after community forest management in 56% of the 524 cases tracking it [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1].
forest_restoration__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: This is a landscape benefit rather than an on-farm one: the biodiversity gain accrues to the restored forest and the landscape around it, not to the adopting farmer's fields. The class follows the sub-practice vote, which tempers the pooled result. Natural regeneration and the cross-practice meta-analysis hold the strongest results [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles16_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles17_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_1]. Assisted regeneration and forest protection and community management read moderate: the assisted-regeneration evidence is perch and practitioner results, and much of the protection evidence is forest cover and governance with mixed outcomes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_loureiro21_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_2325_2017_plant_diversity, ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1]. Active planting is itself conflicted, with Turkmen practitioner ratings and seedling recruitment beneath framework plantings on one side and, on the other, the warning that planting can reduce biodiversity benefits where forest could regenerate [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1529_2012_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wydhayagarn09_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_williams24_1]. The review finding that afforestation in north-west India mostly lost diversity and promoted monocultures has been moved to the plantation family, which is parked out of this roll-up, so it no longer weighs on active planting here. The NbS-level class therefore sits at moderate rather than at the strong reading of the regeneration evidence. Planting is not automatically the better route, and in some settings it is the worse one. Where forests can regenerate naturally or with some assistance, reforestation based on tree planting can actually reduce biodiversity conservation benefits if the selected species or management do not provide suitable habitat for species of conservation concern [ev_biodiversity_outcome_williams24_1]. The gains in this row are measured from cleared, degraded or grazed starting points. Several outcomes did not move: biodiversity in Vietnamese special-use forests showed no clear-cut evidence of a positive project impact, with the tracking tool judged an unsuitable proxy [ev_biodiversity_outcome_ieg18_1]; management transfer under Madagascar's Gelose remained superficial and did not stop clearing [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2]; and broadleaf crown-cover change under Van Panchayats was insignificant [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_2]. The same community-forest analysis found environmental condition decreased in 32% of cases, a large minority [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1]. Harm was measured elsewhere too, though rarely: of 1,924 project locations assessed, 33 (1.7%) showed strong evidence of negative outcomes, all apparently in areas susceptible to urban encroachment, and 169 (8.7%) gave no evidence of a positive outcome [ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_3]. The strength is qualified on other grounds too. Much of the positive weight comes from practitioner ratings on a fixed scale and from forest-cover and governance findings routed in as a component proxy, not from direct biodiversity counts [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1]. And the benefit is not costless on the farm: a compiler who rated wildlife increasing also recorded that this led to danger of wild life on crops and domestic animals [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1414_2011_animal_diversity]. Plantation evidence, including the comparison of plantations and clear-cut regeneration against uncut forest, is reported in the plantation family's own row; that family is kept out of the forest-restoration roll-up and is read separately.

forest_restoration__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: In low and lower-middle income settings the evidence is mainly WOCAT compiler ratings: area closure in Ethiopia brought back wildlife, assisted natural regeneration in Niger and Bangladesh increased plant, animal and habitat diversity as canopy cover and tree density improved, broadleaf plantations in India provide water and habitat for small animals and birds, and protection measures in Khost, Afghanistan saw migratory animals and birds return [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1414_2011_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_4372_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_5243_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_7460_2024_animal_diversity]. Community forest management across community forests in Nepal reduced both poverty and deforestation, retaining habitat [ev_landscape_forest_cover_iufro20_1].
forest_restoration__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: Management transfers in Madagascar remained superficial and did not stop clearing [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2], and the Ethiopian compiler notes that returning wildlife became a danger to crops and domestic animals. No unit in this scope measures species directly: all biodiversity units are compiler ratings and the Nepal and Madagascar units concern forest cover, a component proxy.

forest_restoration__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: This row rests on forest-governance evidence pooled across several countries, with forest cover standing in for habitat. A meta-analysis of payments for environmental services found improved forest cover (SMD = 0.32, 95% CI [0.10, 0.55]) and reduced deforestation (SMD = −0.12) compared with areas without payments [ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_2]. World Bank participatory forest management projects reported reduced deforestation rates, regeneration of degraded forests and protection of biodiversity where those outcomes were monitored, and Bank-supported payment schemes had a positive effect on deforestation in some countries [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_ieg13_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1].
forest_restoration__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: The payment schemes were applied broadly rather than targeting high-value forest areas, which limits what they deliver for biodiversity [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1]. Most units measure forest cover or deforestation, a component proxy for biodiversity, not species. The pooled payment effects come from a systematic review and meta-analysis, while the World Bank units are evaluation narratives that cover only projects that monitored outcomes; all concern keeping or managing existing forest through payments or community management rather than restoration planting.

forest_restoration__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: In these upper-middle-income settings the evidence is about succession on land that has been cleared or degraded, and about what speeds it up. Tree species richness rose as a function of time since disturbance across an Atlantic rainforest chronosequence [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_1], with a forest estimated to need 65 years, range 23 to 178, to reach a proportion of 80% animal-dispersed species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_2]. Assisted recruitment shortens the wait: beneath framework-species plantings in Thai dry forest, tree seedlings of many species recruited, 25 of them animal-dispersed and 11 wind-dispersed [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wydhayagarn09_1], and artificial perches produced native zoochoric regenerants that were absent from planted rings, so bringing in dispersers mattered more than the planting itself [ev_biodiversity_outcome_loureiro21_1]. On Turkmen barkhan sands the revegetated area is recorded as providing habitat for 25-27 species of plants and animals, with plant and animal diversity rated as increasing [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1529_2012_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1529_2012_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1529_2012_animal_diversity]. Holding the cover is the companion mechanism: under community forest management in the Sierra Norte de Puebla, forest cover did not decline after the handover but increased by 8% [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1].
forest_restoration__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: The direction is consistent, but the base is thin and soft: chronosequences and site studies, a set of compiler ratings, and a forest-cover change read from land-use maps as a proxy for habitat rather than a count of species [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1]. Where a project was independently evaluated the result was less flattering — biodiversity is hard to assess, the management-effectiveness tool used was not a suitable proxy, and there was no clear-cut evidence that a Vietnamese special-use forest project had a positive impact [ev_biodiversity_outcome_ieg18_1]. Time is the binding condition: the Atlantic-forest estimate spans decades to well over a century before the assemblage approaches the composition of a mature forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_2], so nothing here promises a measurable result inside a project cycle. Two reading rules apply. The gains are measured against the degraded or cleared starting point, not against intact forest, and a young stand holding less than old-growth is incomplete recovery rather than loss. And the perch and framework-species findings are about assisting dispersal into a restoration site [ev_biodiversity_outcome_loureiro21_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wydhayagarn09_1]: they presuppose a seed source within reach, which is a siting condition a scan can test and a restoration in a cleared landscape may fail.

forest_restoration__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: Across the restoration families taken together, carbon gains are real but uneven between families; they accrue in two pools: biomass as the trees grow, and soil organic carbon after the land-use transition. On biomass, natural regeneration removed 9.1 to 18.8 t CO2 per hectare per year during the first 20 years of growth [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_3]. Stock estimates line up with those rates: a 20-year-old secondary natural forest in the moist tropical biome was estimated at 51 t of aboveground carbon per hectare [ev_carbon_sequestration_busch19_1], the median present value of 30-year accumulation from natural regeneration is 60.2 tC per hectare in above- and belowground biomass and soil [ev_carbon_sequestration_busch24_1], and regeneration over 215 Mha could sequester 23.4 Gt of carbon in aboveground biomass over 30 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_williams24_1]. Measured plantings show the accumulation directly: native-species restoration on former pasture held 21.85, 25.78 and 38.29 t C per hectare at three, five and seven years [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_3], and intervention sites were sequestering approximately 1.33 tons of carbon per hectare per year more than without the project [ev_carbon_sequestration_gefieo19_1]. On soils, across 151 transitions to forest the average carbon gain was 0.447% of pre-transition soil carbon per year [ev_soil_organic_carbon_busch19_1], and practitioners across Niger, India, Tunisia, Bangladesh and Eritrea rate soil organic matter and above-ground biomass as rising under these technologies [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_2325_2017_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_5243_2019_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_1568_2013_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_4372_2019_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_1330_2010_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_2325_2017_biomass_above_ground_C]. A review of nature-based solutions adds that afforestation increases topsoil carbon in carbon-poor soils [ev_soil_organic_carbon_seddon21_5]. Avoided loss carries the rest: keeping existing cover through community management, payments and project support is counted here as retained carbon [ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_iufro20_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_2], and environmental condition improved after community forest management in 56% of the 524 cases tracking it in a global analysis [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1].
forest_restoration__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: The biomass figures are growth rates over the first decades, not a permanent stock. A young restoration is also far from the reference it is growing towards — the same Atlantic-forest study that measured 21.85 to 38.29 t C per hectare in plantings aged three to seven years measured 138.94 in the mature forest [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_3] — which is incomplete recovery against intact forest, while the gain being claimed is against the pasture the planting replaced. Delivery is not guaranteed by the instrument: a REDD+ pilot in Nepal had an insignificant effect on total forest carbon [ev_carbon_sequestration_snilstveit19_1], management transfers in Madagascar did not halt clearing [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2], crown-cover gains in broadleaf forests under community management were insignificant [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_2], of 1,924 assessed project locations 33 showed strong evidence of negative outcomes and 169 no evidence of a positive one [ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_3], and environmental condition decreased in 32% of community-forest cases [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1]. Planting can also lose carbon: the same review that reports topsoil gains in carbon-poor soils states that the associated soil disturbance causes significant losses in carbon-rich soils, especially of the deep soil carbon that takes many decades to accumulate [ev_soil_organic_carbon_seddon21_5], that afforestation on peaty soils can lead to losses of soil carbon that outweigh that sequestered as the trees grow [ev_carbon_sequestration_seddon21_7]. Those are review sentences carrying cited findings, and they mark where planting reverses the sign: carbon-rich and peaty soils. Finally, weigh the mix: the largest totals are modelled potentials over large areas [ev_carbon_sequestration_williams24_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_busch24_1], a substantial share of the supporting units are compiler ratings on a fixed scale rather than measurements, and forest cover enters as a component proxy for carbon rather than as a stock measurement [ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_1]. The strongest carbon numbers in the wider evidence belong to the plantation family — the afforestation soil-carbon meta-analysis and the plantation biomass and harvest-cycle figures — and plantations are tree farming rather than restoration, so they are reported in their own row outside this roll-up and do not count here; that is why this row reads more cautiously than a pooled reading would. Across those families the picture is uneven: regeneration-based families carry the larger measured and modelled accumulation, while active planting and community protection carry the smaller and more mixed results above. How much soil carbon is gained by land-use history, climate zone or soil type is not resolved in this row. The carbon is a landscape and climate benefit, accruing off-site rather than as a return on the farmer's own plot.

forest_restoration__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: In low and lower-middle income settings, WOCAT compilers rate biomass and soil carbon as increased under assisted natural regeneration in Niger and Bangladesh, broadleaf plantations in India, area closure with Acacia reforestation in Tunisia, enclosures with controlled burning in Tanzania, afforestation in Eritrea, reforestation in Honduras and protection in Khost, Afghanistan [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_2325_2017_biomass_above_ground_C, ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_5243_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_1568_2013_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_1607_2014_biomass_above_ground_C]. Community forest management in Nepal retained forest cover by reducing deforestation [ev_landscape_forest_cover_iufro20_1], and a global analysis of community forests found environmental condition improved after community forest management in 56% of the 524 cases tracking it [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1]. In a systematic review of decentralised forest management, community-managed Van Panchayats in India improved the annual forest cover change rate by 0.40 percentage points, and decentralised administration of protected forests in Bolivia by 0.80 percentage points [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_3].
forest_restoration__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: No unit in this scope measures carbon stocks or rates: the carbon units are compiler ratings, and forest cover and soil organic matter enter as component proxies. Community management transfers in Madagascar did not stop clearing [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2], and in the global community-forest analysis environmental condition decreased in 32% of cases [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1]. The one unit that measures carbon directly finds no gain: the REDD+ pilot in Nepal had an insignificant effect on total forest carbon in community forests (SMD = 0.09) [ev_carbon_sequestration_snilstveit19_1]. Under Van Panchayats the change in broadleaf crown cover was also insignificant (0.026 percentage points) [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_2]; the Indian, Bolivian and Nepal results are cited in systematic reviews.

forest_restoration__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: This row rests on forest-governance evidence pooled across several countries, with forest cover standing in for carbon kept in standing forest. A meta-analysis of payments for environmental services found improved forest cover (SMD = 0.32, 95% CI [0.10, 0.55]) and reduced deforestation (SMD = −0.12) against comparison areas [ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_2]. World Bank participatory forest management projects reported reduced deforestation rates and regeneration of degraded forests where those outcomes were monitored, and Bank-supported payment schemes had a positive effect on deforestation in some countries [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_2, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1].
forest_restoration__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: No unit measures carbon stocks or sequestration rates: all four measure forest cover or deforestation, a component proxy. The payment schemes were applied broadly rather than targeting high-value forest areas [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1]. The pooled payment effects come from a systematic review and meta-analysis, the World Bank units are evaluation narratives covering only projects that monitored outcomes, and all concern keeping existing forest through payments or community management rather than restoration.

forest_restoration__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: In upper-middle-income settings the measured evidence is a native-species restoration on former pasture in Brazil's Atlantic Forest, which held 21.85, 25.78 and 38.29 Mg of carbon per hectare at three, five and seven years [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_3]. Under community forest management in Mexico's Sierra Norte de Puebla forest cover did not undergo any loss and increased by 8%, which enters here as retained and added cover rather than a carbon stock [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1]. WOCAT compilers rate above-ground biomass carbon as strongly increased for dune afforestation in Turkmenistan, expecting the numbers to be achieved on the sand dunes in 3 years, and soil organic matter as increased under afforestation in Cabo Verde and in karst areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_1529_2012_biomass_above_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_1523_2011_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_4367_2019_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C].
forest_restoration__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: The same Atlantic-forest study measured 138.94 Mg of carbon per hectare in the mature forest, so the seven-year planting is far from its reference: that is incomplete recovery against intact forest, while the gain claimed is against the pasture the planting replaced [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_3]. The Mexican result is a before-and-after reading of land-use maps with no counterfactual, a proxy for carbon [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1], and the WOCAT units are compiler ratings on a fixed scale rather than measurements.

forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.mechanism: This row asks how much water leaves the catchment after forest cover is restored or expanded, and the evidence finds both less and more, with close to even weight on each side. Measured syntheses mostly find less: in about 80% of study cases reporting annual water yields the effect of forest restoration and other forms of forest cover expansion was negative, and in 6% positive [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1]; baseflow decreased in 63% of cases [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_2]; groundwater levels or recharge decreased with forest cover expansion in 67% of the studies reporting them [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_filoso17_1]; and no study in the meta-analysis subset showed a water-yield gain [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_3]. A global review found a significant negative relationship between forest cover gain and annual runoff in large watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_3]. The reason given is interception and use: tropical forest canopies commonly intercept up to 35 per cent of rainfall, and much of the water that soaks in is used by the trees [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1]. An FAO synthesis states that the effects of reforestation or afforestation on water yields are usually the reverse of those for forest removal, that low flows are usually diminished as well, especially where fast-growing, heavy water-using species are employed, and that planting forests on open land where the water table is close to the surface will lower groundwater levels [ev_water_yield_ham08_5, ev_water_yield_ham08_6, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_2]; after clearance, the streamflow gain declines as new cover establishes, and a return to pre-cut totals under natural regrowth may take more than eight years [ev_water_yield_ham08_8]. Planting shows the same: a cited New Zealand study notes afforestation reducing water yield while giving erosion benefits [ev_water_regulation_iufro18_4]; a global review warns that large-scale afforestation in water-limited environments will inevitably exacerbate water scarcity [ev_water_yield_zhang17_7]. On the gain side, baseflow from Ethiopian catchments with exclosures was 1.5 to 4 times greater than from cropland [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1]; a regional land-climate model projects significant increases of 11.4%, 16.9%, 17.6% and 84.9% in four regions under full reforestation potential [ev_water_regulation_teo22_1, ev_water_regulation_teo22_2, ev_water_regulation_teo22_3, ev_water_regulation_teo22_4]; about 19 small watersheds and a large watershed showed increased annual runoff due to forest cover gain, and spruce reforestation of a Heihe River headwater was predicted to increase annual runoff by 8.6% for a 12.6% increase in forest cover [ev_water_yield_zhang17_5, ev_water_yield_zhang17_6]; and forest succession and declining evapotranspiration may explain increased summer streamflow at two temperate forest sites logged in the early nineteenth century [ev_water_yield_jon12_3].
forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.conditionality: What separates the sides is baseline, method, species and time. The losses come from measured syntheses that pool forest restoration with other forms of forest cover expansion [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1], from reviews of reforestation and afforestation, and from planting with fast-growing, heavy water-using species [ev_water_yield_ham08_6]. The gains are an exclosure-versus-cropland contrast rather than a comparison with unrestored land [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1], model projections at regional scale that work through precipitation as well as evapotranspiration [ev_water_regulation_teo22_1, ev_water_yield_zhang17_6], a minority of watersheds in a global review [ev_water_yield_zhang17_5], and a tentative attribution at sites logged in the early nineteenth century [ev_water_yield_jon12_3]. Some regions in the same model show nonsignificant declines where heightened evapotranspiration outstrips increases in precipitation [ev_water_regulation_teo22_5]. Several units are nulls: the global review failed to detect a statistically significant relationship between forest cover gain and annual runoff in small watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_2], and an FAO–CIFOR review states that interception should put to rest the belief that extensive reforestation or afforestation will increase low flows in the dry season [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1]. Scale matters within the losses too: the decrease shrinks at larger temporal and spatial scales in the systematic review [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_3], while the global review finds the runoff reduction significant only in large watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_3]. The lowered water table under new forest is also described as improving drainage, so on waterlogged open land it is not purely a loss [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_2]. The review report that China's Grain-for-Green programme, planted mainly with fast-growing non-native species, reduced water supply has been re-homed to the plantation family, which is parked out of this roll-up; without that loss inside the restoration families the pool no longer leans negative, so no direction is stated. This row is for downstream users and basin planners: a loss here can coexist with local supply gains reported in the forest restoration water stress row, so read the two side by side rather than netting one against the other. Plantation results are reported in their own family row and do not count here.

forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.mechanism: At long-term ecological research sites in the USA, forest succession and declining evapotranspiration may explain increased summer streamflow at two temperate forest sites that were logged in the early nineteenth century [ev_water_yield_jon12_3]. Against it, a cited New Zealand study notes that afforestation can provide relevant erosion reduction benefits while reducing water yield [ev_water_regulation_iufro18_4].
forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.conditionality: What separates the two is the practice and the time scale: the gain is summer flow at sites logged in the early nineteenth century and left to forest succession, while the loss is afforestation, cited without a time frame [ev_water_yield_jon12_3, ev_water_regulation_iufro18_4]. Both are thin. The US attribution is tentative in the authors' own wording, and no intervention is described at those sites; the New Zealand unit is a modelled trade-off carried from a study the assessment cites. Neither gives a size, and neither comes from the low- and lower-middle-income target. This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment.

forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.mechanism: In the two lower-income contexts in this scope, the evidence reads the other way from the pooled syntheses: baseflow from Ethiopian catchments with exclosures was 1.5 to 4 times greater than baseflow from cropland [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1], and a regional land-climate model projects a significant 84.9% increase in water yield for the Irrawaddy under full reforestation potential by mid-century [ev_water_regulation_teo22_4].
forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.conditionality: This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment, not whether the restored land itself holds more. Neither unit measures restored forest against the land it replaced: the Ethiopian figure compares exclosure catchments with cropland, and the Irrawaddy figure is a mid-century model scenario at landscape scale, not a project observation. Read it alongside the unscoped catchment water yield row, which pools the wider measured evidence, before treating restoration in a lower-income catchment as a source of extra downstream water.

forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.mechanism: Afforesting grasslands and shrublands, mostly with pine and eucalypt plantations in paired catchments, reduced annual runoff on average by 44% and 31% respectively, with proportionally even larger reductions for low flow, and losses far greater at the driest grassland site, at 62% [ev_water_yield_farley05_1, ev_water_yield_farley05_2, ev_water_yield_farley05_3, ev_water_yield_farley05_4]. Tropical forest canopies commonly intercept up to 35 per cent of rainfall, which evaporates without reaching soil water reserves, and much of the water that does soak in is used by the trees themselves [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1].
forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.conditionality: This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment, not whether the restored land itself holds more. A loss here can coexist with a local gain in the water stress rows, since the trees use much of the water that soaks in [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1]. The evidence is afforestation of grassland and shrubland, mostly in South Africa, Australia and New Zealand, and the authors suggest the effects on water yield will be more severe in drier regions [ev_water_yield_farley05_4]. The FAO–CIFOR synthesis concludes that extensive reforestation or afforestation should not be expected to increase dry-season low flows [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1].

forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.mechanism: In China the evidence is modelled. A regional land-climate model under full reforestation potential projects statistically significant water-yield increases of 11.4% on the Loess Plateau–North China Plain, 16.9% on the Yangtze Plain and 17.6% in Southeast China [ev_water_regulation_teo22_1, ev_water_regulation_teo22_2, ev_water_regulation_teo22_3], and in the headwater of the Heihe River Basin a 12.6% increase in forest cover due to spruce reforestation was predicted to increase annual runoff by 8.6% [ev_water_yield_zhang17_6].
forest_restoration__catchment_water_yiel.conditionality: Every unit is a projection: the gains are scenario results for full reforestation potential, the Heihe figure is cited from an earlier modelling study, and the regional model works through precipitation as well as evapotranspiration, not only through what the trees use [ev_water_regulation_teo22_1, ev_water_yield_zhang17_6]. Read the class as what large reforestation could do in modelled scenarios, not as a measured project outcome. The one programme result from China, the review report that Grain-for-Green planting with mainly fast-growing non-native species reduced water supply, has been re-homed to the plantation family, which is parked out of the forest-restoration roll-up; it remains the warning on species choice, and that row should be read before assuming a gain. All units are from China. This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment.

forest_restoration__cost_per_hectare_res.mechanism: Cost per hectare depends mainly on method: modelled implementation cost has a median of US$140/ha for natural regeneration [ev_project_cost_busch24_1], natural regeneration methods are cited at US$12-3,880/ha against US$105-25,830/ha for restoration projects in the tropics and subtropics [ev_project_cost_williams24_2], and natural regeneration in Uganda is tabled at US$26/ha [ev_project_cost_wri17_5]. A Brazilian cost survey reports the same gap: direct seeding and seedling planting cost approximately ten times more (about US$2000/ha) than natural and assisted regeneration and enrichment planting (about US$200/ha), mostly due to the higher input costs [ev_project_cost_branc19_1, ev_project_cost_branc19_2, ev_project_cost_branc19_3]. The opportunity cost of land (median US$4,807/ha) is generally higher and more variable than implementation cost [ev_project_cost_busch24_5].
forest_restoration__cost_per_hectare_res.conditionality: Most reported figures state no price year, some are assumptions rather than observed costs [ev_project_cost_wri17_1], and WOCAT values are compiler-entered conversions from local currency. Values from high-income and upper-middle-income settings, including the Brazilian survey figures, are excluded from the low and lower-middle income range. Plantation results are reported in their own family rows and no longer count toward forest restoration.

forest_restoration__cost_per_hectare_res.mechanism: In low and lower-middle income settings, costs are lowest where existing regrowth is used: natural regeneration in Uganda at US$26/ha and assisted natural regeneration in Niger and Bangladesh at US$90/ha and US$197.62/ha [ev_project_cost_wri17_5, ev_project_cost_wocat_2325_2017_establishment, ev_project_cost_wocat_4372_2019_establishment]. Planting-based work costs more, from rain forest corridor planting in Madagascar (US$938/ha), community forest management in Benin, broadleaf plantations in India and the Khost learning site in Afghanistan to community microbasin reforestation in Honduras at US$5,402.39/ha [ev_project_cost_wri17_4, ev_project_cost_wri17_2, ev_project_cost_wocat_750_2016_establishment].
forest_restoration__cost_per_hectare_res.conditionality: The table and cited values give no price year and the WOCAT values are compiler conversions from local-currency entries.

forest_restoration__cost_per_tco2e_avoid.mechanism: Abatement cost compares implementation and land opportunity costs with the carbon gained: modelled natural regeneration costs a median of US$23.80 per tCO2 [ev_project_cost_busch24_3]. In Colombia's western Andes a median carbon price of US$1.99 per tCO2 over 30 years was enough to compensate landowners for letting pastures regenerate [ev_project_cost_chazdon16_1], and conserving 90% of remaining mangroves could be achieved at carbon prices between 3.0 and 13.0 US$ per tCO2 [ev_project_cost_jakovac20_2]. Two payment schemes report low programme costs per tonne of carbon: the PAS scheme in Brazil was estimated at 0.56 USD per ton of CO2, and the Ugandan scheme cost $0.57 per ton of delayed emissions against an estimated social benefit of $1.11 per ton, roughly two times the cost [ev_project_cost_snilstveit19_2, ev_project_cost_snilstveit19_3].
forest_restoration__cost_per_tco2e_avoid.conditionality: All units are modelled or break-even prices rather than project budgets, and the mangrove conservation figure concerns avoided emissions from protecting existing forest rather than restoration; the Colombian figure is cited from another study and states no price year. The Brazilian figure is a total programme cost given without assessing cost-effectiveness, both payment figures are cited in a systematic review, and both concern paying landholders to keep existing forest rather than restoring it [ev_project_cost_snilstveit19_2, ev_project_cost_snilstveit19_3]. Plantation results are reported in their own family rows and no longer count toward forest restoration.

forest_restoration__cost_reduction.mechanism: Natural regeneration lowers cost by letting forests grow back on their own or with low-cost assistance, cited at US$12-3,880/ha against US$105-25,830/ha for restoration projects, and is often more effective than full tree planting in long-term success [ev_project_cost_williams24_1]; European guidelines likewise note its lower cost and locally adapted genetic material [ev_project_cost_stanturf26_1]. In a mulching experiment in tropical dry deciduous forest on Mexico's Jalisco coast, polyethylene mulch cut the cost of each established plant, including nursery costs, from 18.00 USD on bare soil to 2.45 USD, because 92 of 180 plants established against 10 of 180 without mulch [ev_project_cost_barajas13_1]. Decentralised administration of Van Panchayat forests in India is associated with costs approximately 1/13th of those under state administration [ev_project_cost_samii14_1].
forest_restoration__cost_reduction.conditionality: The European statement is an expert assertion that also notes limits in species composition, and the cost comparison is a cited range without price year. Organic mulches cut cost per established plant less, to 12.50 USD with alfalfa straw and 13.33 USD with leaf litter, and the result comes from a single experiment at one site [ev_project_cost_barajas13_1]; the Van Panchayat cost figure is cited in a systematic review and concerns administering existing forest [ev_project_cost_samii14_1].

forest_restoration__cost_reduction__inco.mechanism: Measures taken at planting can cut the cost of each tree that survives. In a Mexican tropical dry forest, polyethylene mulch raised establishment from 10 of 180 unmulched plants to 92 of 180 and brought the cost per established plant down from USD 18.00 to USD 2.45, nursery costs included; alfalfa straw and leaf litter cost more material and established fewer plants, at USD 12.50 and USD 13.33 per plant [ev_project_cost_barajas13_1]. At the other end of the scale, a successful black-mangrove project in Tabasco reforested 50 ha at USD 3,945.60 per hectare, a figure that covers sanitation, dredging, soil conservation works, ridge restoration, training, plant production, transplanting and monitoring [ev_project_cost_hernmel17_2].
forest_restoration__cost_reduction__inco.conditionality: The two figures are not comparable and neither is a cost saving on its own: the mulch result is a cost per surviving plant from a single trial on three species, while the mangrove figure is a whole-project cost per hectare for one site, reported in a diagnostic study without a comparison against a cheaper alternative [ev_project_cost_barajas13_1, ev_project_cost_hernmel17_2]. Both come from Mexico, an upper-middle-income setting, so they say little about what the same works would cost elsewhere, and the mangrove cost is a second-hand figure attributed to a local project record [ev_project_cost_hernmel17_2].

forest_restoration__cross_family__biodiv.mechanism: A global meta-analysis of 221 study landscapes found that forest restoration enhances biodiversity by 15 to 84% and vegetation structure by 36 to 77% compared with degraded ecosystems, as regrowing forest rebuilds habitat structure [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles16_1].
forest_restoration__cross_family__biodiv.conditionality: This rests on a single meta-analysis in which restored sites are secondary or selectively logged forests and active and passive restoration are not separated, so it cannot attribute the gain to a particular restoration family.

forest_restoration__cross_family__catchm.mechanism: A global systematic review pooling forest restoration with forestry and afforestation found that annual water yield decreased in about 80% of study cases reporting it and increased in 6% [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1], baseflow decreased in 63% of cases [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_2], groundwater levels or recharge decreased in 67% of the studies reporting them [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_filoso17_1], and no water-yield gains were observed in the meta-analysed subset [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_3]. A global review of forest change found a significant negative relationship between forest cover gain and annual runoff in large watersheds, so the reduction is only significant there [ev_water_yield_zhang17_3]. Tropical forest canopies commonly intercept up to 35 per cent of rainfall, which evaporates without reaching soil water reserves, and much of the water that does soak in is used by the trees themselves [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1].
forest_restoration__cross_family__catchm.conditionality: This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment, with groundwater recharge counted as a component, not whether the restored land itself holds more. Local supply sits in the water stress rows, and a loss here can coexist with a gain there, since the trees use much of the water that soaks in [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1]. The two syntheses read scale differently: in the systematic review the decrease shrinks at larger temporal and spatial scales [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_3], while the global review failed to detect a statistically significant relationship in small watersheds and found the reduction significant only in large ones [ev_water_yield_zhang17_2, ev_water_yield_zhang17_3]. The same global review records about 19 small watersheds and a large watershed with increased annual runoff due to forest cover gain, a minority reversal of the usual direction [ev_water_yield_zhang17_5]. Both reviews pool restoration with other forms of forest cover gain; the systematic review reports vote counts rather than pooled sizes, is dominated by temperate and Oceania studies, and the baseflow cases are few [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_2]. One further unit is carried but does not vote: by 25 to 35 years after forest harvest in temperate basins, summer streamflow declined by up to 30%–50% relative to the reference basins [ev_water_yield_jon12_1]. Its comparator is intact old forest, not unrestored land similar to the starting point before regrowth, so it measures how far regenerating forest falls short of the reference rather than what restoration changes; it is a recovery shortfall and is kept out of the class.

forest_restoration__cross_family__cost_p.mechanism: Across restoration families, the opportunity cost of land is generally higher and more variable than implementation cost, with a modelled median of US$4,807/ha [ev_project_cost_busch24_5]; restoration projects in the tropics and subtropics are cited at US$105-25,830/ha [ev_project_cost_williams24_2] and the TEEB study assumed US$2,390-3,450/ha [ev_project_cost_wri17_1].
forest_restoration__cross_family__cost_p.conditionality: These are modelled, cited or assumed values rather than observed project costs, none states a price year, and they pool restoration methods without separating families.

forest_restoration__cross_family__drough.mechanism: A meta-analysis of catchment restoration in Ethiopia reports that exclosures, tree planting, bunds and terraces reduce water losses and improve the quantity and quality of water in soils, rivers and aquifers, a pathway to drought resilience [ev_soil_water_retention_meaza22_1].
forest_restoration__cross_family__drough.conditionality: This is a single source on soil and stream water, a component of drought impact rather than a drought outcome, and it pools exclosure and planting with soil and water conservation structures, so the share due to tree restoration is not isolated [ev_soil_water_retention_meaza22_1].

forest_restoration__cross_family__flood_.mechanism: A global systematic review found that flooding or peak flows decreased with forest cover expansion in 82% of the studies with data on them [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]. A harvest experiment in Oregon adds a measured recovery: after clear-cutting, peak discharges recovered gradually over time as the basin revegetated, which the authors attribute to changes in evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5].
forest_restoration__cross_family__flood_.conditionality: The review pools explicit and implicit forest restoration with forestry and afforestation and reports vote counts rather than effect sizes, so it does not say how large the reduction is or which restoration practice delivers it [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]. The Oregon recovery is measured against the freshly cut state in a harvest study, not against long-degraded land, and the paper does not say whether the regrowth was planted or natural [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. No unit comes from a low- or lower-middle-income setting. Expert positions point the other way: an FAO–CIFOR synthesis concludes that massive forestation programmes proclaimed as the answer to preventing floods simply will not do the job, although reforestation may bring other benefits [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_3], and a published comment argues that reforestation does not necessarily reduce flooding if soil properties do not recover, river bed morphology does not change and settlements, roads and drains remain unaltered [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_5]. Neither is a measurement; what separates them from the positive side is that they address flood prevention at large scale, while the review and the Oregon basin report peak flows in study catchments. No unit covers severe or extreme flood. For farmers the effect is off-site.

forest_restoration__cross_family__flood_.mechanism: Flooding or peak flows decreased with forest cover expansion in 82% of the studies with data on them in a global systematic review, consistent with forest cover slowing storm runoff [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1], and in a US experimental basin the gradual recovery of peak discharges after clear-cutting, as vegetation regrew, is attributed to changes in evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5].
forest_restoration__cross_family__flood_.conditionality: The review pools explicit and implicit forest restoration with forestry and afforestation, is dominated by temperate and Oceania studies, and reports vote counts rather than effect sizes, so it does not say how large the reduction is or which restoration practice delivers it [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]; the US result is regrowth after a clear-cut, not a restoration project, and does not name a practice [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. No unit comes from a low- or lower-middle-income setting. Expert positions point the other way: an FAO–CIFOR synthesis concludes that massive forestation programmes proclaimed as the answer to preventing floods simply will not do the job, although reforestation may bring other benefits [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_3], and a published comment argues that reforestation does not necessarily reduce flooding if soil properties do not recover, river bed morphology does not change and settlements, roads and drains remain [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_5]. Neither is a measurement. Any benefit is off-site for farmers.

forest_restoration__cross_family__heat_s.mechanism: Satellite comparisons of forest gain and loss show that more forest cools the land surface locally in tropical and temperate regions, with the largest cooling where tropical forest cover rose by about 50%, while forest loss warms it [ev_microclimate_buffering_prevedello19_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_prevedello19_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_prevedello19_5].
forest_restoration__cross_family__heat_s.conditionality: The cooling is absent in boreal regions [ev_microclimate_buffering_prevedello19_3]. The evidence is a single global remote-sensing study of observed forest-cover change, not of planting or regeneration as such, and land surface temperature is only a proxy for heat stress.

forest_restoration__cross_family__heat_s.mechanism: Gaining forest cover cools the land surface: forestation lowered annual land surface temperature by 0.18 degC in the tropics and 0.19 degC in temperate regions, and forestation of about 50% in tropical regions led to cooling of 1.11 degC, while deforestation warmed the tropics by 0.38 degC [ev_microclimate_buffering_prevedello19_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_prevedello19_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_prevedello19_5].
forest_restoration__cross_family__heat_s.conditionality: Boreal regions showed a null effect [ev_microclimate_buffering_prevedello19_3]. The source is a single remote-sensing study of observed forest-cover change rather than a named restoration practice, it measures annual land surface temperature rather than heat extremes, and microclimate buffering enters as a component of heat-stress hazard.

forest_restoration__cross_family__produc.mechanism: Under the Reflorestar payment programme in Espírito Santo, Brazil, the poorest quarter of municipalities saw agricultural value added rise by 8% and the value of agricultural production by about 14% [ev_agricultural_production_value_seixas24_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_seixas24_3].
forest_restoration__cross_family__produc.conditionality: The gain holds only for the poorest municipalities; the better-off municipalities showed a 14% decline, and aggregate municipal indicators showed no significant effect. The programme pools standing-forest conservation with regeneration, planting, agroforestry and silvopasture, and municipal production value is a proxy for the farm production gap in an upper-middle income setting.

forest_restoration__cross_family__rural_.mechanism: Restored forests can diversify livelihoods and raise income from timber and non-timber forest products [ev_household_income_iufro20_8]; in Wuqi County, China, the sloping land conservation programme increased local incomes by 164 percent and off-farm income by 20 times [ev_household_income_wri17_1], and global estimates put the benefit-cost ratio of restoring degraded forest land at 7.5 to 30.9, including public goods [ev_economic_return_wri17_1, ev_economic_return_wri17_2]. A meta-analysis of payment-for-environmental-services programmes finds a positive effect on overall household income (SMD = 0.25, 95% CI [0.09, 0.41]) [ev_household_income_snilstveit19_1].
forest_restoration__cross_family__rural_.conditionality: Restoration can also take agricultural land and reduce on-farm income or employment [ev_household_income_iufro20_7], few studies conclusively show that restored-forest benefits alleviate poverty, which occurs over years or decades when it does [ev_rural_poverty_iufro20_4], and Brazil's Reflorestar programme showed no significant effect on municipal GDP, value added or employment [ev_economic_return_seixas24_1]. The Wuqi gain is ex post without a counterfactual and largely off-farm and subsidy-driven, the benefit-cost ratios are global model estimates, and income and returns are proxies for poverty. The same meta-analysis finds no significant effect on income from agricultural sources (SMD = 0.11), on nonagricultural income or on household assets [ev_household_income_snilstveit19_2], so the income gain does not show up as farm income or wealth.

forest_restoration__cross_family__soil_e.mechanism: Review statements that name restoration generically, not a single family, sit here. An FAO regional review of forests and landslides in Asia asserts that tree planting on susceptible slopes can reduce risk, and that natural regeneration and tree planting on failed slopes can help control after-effects such as sediment release into rivers [ev_erosion_hazard_forbes11_1]. An FAO forests-and-water synthesis calls forest restoration one of the best ways of restoring productivity and reducing sedimentation in degraded areas of cleared land experiencing accelerated erosion [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_1], and lists reducing soil loss and keeping sediment out of streams among the very good reasons for rehabilitating watersheds [ev_erosion_hazard_ham08_1]. It cites Taiwan, where reservoir sedimentation from 1965 until 1985 was reduced by 55 percent of the base rate, attributed to a rehabilitation programme [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. The effect is off-site for farmers: stabilised slopes and less sediment reaching rivers and reservoirs, at slope and catchment scale rather than on the farm plot.
forest_restoration__cross_family__soil_e.conditionality: Only the Taiwan unit says how large the effect is, which is why the class is capped; the other statements are FAO assertions without a measured value. The Taiwan reduction is credited to a bundled programme of reforestation with soil conservation on cultivated land, fire control, check dams and gully control, fruit trees and agroforestry, and conservation farming, so it cannot be attributed to forest restoration alone [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. The same synthesis is explicit that achieving substantial flood reduction is not among the reasons to rehabilitate watersheds [ev_erosion_hazard_ham08_1]. No unit comes from a low- or lower-middle-income setting. The primary landslide and watershed studies behind the Asia review are now registered in their own rows (passive regeneration, active planting and protection). Landslide risk is recorded under erosion here for lack of a landslide category.

forest_restoration__cross_family__water_.mechanism: Both units come from a single FAO forests-and-water synthesis that names restoration generically rather than a single family: forest restoration is described as one of the best ways of restoring productivity and reducing sedimentation in degraded areas of cleared land experiencing accelerated erosion [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_1], and in Taiwan reservoir sedimentation from 1965 until 1985 was reduced by 55 percent of the base rate, attributed to a rehabilitation programme [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. Lower sediment load is used here as a component of water quality, and the benefit falls downstream, off-site for farmers.
forest_restoration__cross_family__water_.conditionality: This row is data deficient: it rests on one source, whose general claim is an assertion and whose Taiwan figure is cited second-hand, so it is described here but cannot set a class. The Taiwan programme bundles reforestation with soil conservation on cultivated land, fire control, check dams and gully control, fruit trees and agroforestry, and conservation farming, so the reduction cannot be credited to restoration alone, and it is a high-income case [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. What is missing is a second independent source or a measured water-quality finding, ideally from a low- or lower-middle-income catchment.

forest_restoration__cross_family__water_.mechanism: Expanding forest cover moves water in two opposite directions within the same review. More water gets into the soil: in 83% of the studies reporting on infiltration capacity or soil infiltration, infiltration increased [ev_soil_permeability_filoso17_1]. Less reaches groundwater: in 67% of the studies with data on groundwater levels or recharge, groundwater decreased with forest cover expansion [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_filoso17_1].
forest_restoration__cross_family__water_.conditionality: The two sides are measuring different things, soil infiltration and groundwater, and the evidence does not say which drives water stress for a given user. A farmer depending on soil moisture and a household depending on wells or springs fed by recharge would read them differently; the groundwater decrease is a measured harm for the latter. Timing also separates them: aboveground benefits recover within a few years, but infiltration and recharge are counted in decades rather than years [ev_soil_permeability_iufro18_1], an expert panel conclusion rather than a measurement. The review pools forestry and afforestation with restoration, is dominated by temperate and Oceania studies, and reports vote counts rather than sizes. Water leaving the catchment for downstream users is covered by the catchment water yield rows.

forest_restoration__drought__all.mechanism: Every sub-practice row that votes here finds forest restoration eases drought only a little, and that agreement on a low effect, not the pooled count of positive units, sets the class. In the protection and community forest management row, the India compiler credits broadleaf plantations, assisted tree regeneration and fodder nurseries with improved surface and subsurface hydrological functioning in the upper watershed, which raised springshed groundwater stores and dry-season stream and spring flows, while the Afghanistan compiler rates drought impacts only slightly reduced [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_5243_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_7460_2024_drought_impacts]. In the passive regeneration row, households in Tigray, Ethiopia, downstream of exclosures harvested 188 to 222 kg/ha more than households beside open grazing areas in the drought-affected 2023 season [ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_1]. The cross-family row rests on a meta-analysis of Ethiopian catchment restoration reporting that exclosures, tree planting, bunds and terraces reduce water losses and improve water in soils, rivers and aquifers [ev_soil_water_retention_meaza22_1]. The pool also holds a Niger rating that assisted natural regeneration helps reduce the impacts of long droughts in the rainy season, and a regional model of large-scale reforestation in the Asia-Pacific that found fewer extremely dry months in 9 of 15 regions [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_2325_2017_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_teo22_1]; the engine's vote names only the cross-family, passive regeneration and protection rows.
forest_restoration__drought__all.conditionality: The effect is off-site for farmers: the Tigray yield advantage compares exclosures with open grazing, so it measures a downstream benefit to cropland rather than production on the restored land, and it was larger in the drier first year than in the following year [ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_3]. The cross-family evidence bundles exclosure and planting with bunds and terraces, the India and Afghanistan sheets bundle planting, regeneration and protection, and the WOCAT units are compiler ratings, not measurements [ev_soil_water_retention_meaza22_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_7460_2024_drought_impacts]. The modelled benefit is landscape-scale only and the source notes that most regional changes were not significant, so it does not speak to plot-scale restoration [ev_drought_hazard_teo22_1].

forest_restoration__drought__all__income.mechanism: Compilers rate afforestation in Cabo Verde as raising soil moisture and off-site water availability, and afforestation of bare karst land in Bosnia and Herzegovina as slightly improving water availability and water collection [ev_soil_water_retention_wocat_1523_2011_soil_moisture, ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1523_2011_water_availability, ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_4367_2019_water_availability].
forest_restoration__drought__all__income.conditionality: This upper-middle-income slice rests on practitioner ratings from very few technology sheets, all of them water proxies rather than a drought-impact rating or measurement. The sheets state no mechanism, so the link from more soil water to lower drought impact is inferred through the proxy, not observed.

forest_restoration__drought__mixed_crop_.mechanism: The India compiler credits a programme of broadleaf plantations, assisted tree regeneration and fodder nurseries with improved surface and subsurface hydrological functioning in the upper watershed, which raised springshed groundwater stores and dry-season stream and spring flows, and the Niger compiler credits assisted natural regeneration with improving vegetation cover and woody production that help reduce the impacts of long droughts in the rainy season [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_5243_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_2325_2017_drought_impacts]. In Tigray, Ethiopia, households downstream of exclosures harvested 188 to 222 kg/ha more than households beside open grazing areas in the drought-affected 2023 season, and a meta-analysis of Ethiopian catchment restoration reports that exclosures, tree planting, bunds and terraces reduce water losses and improve water in soils, rivers and aquifers [ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_1, ev_soil_water_retention_meaza22_1]. A regional model of large-scale reforestation in water-insecure parts of the Asia-Pacific found fewer extremely dry months in 9 of 15 regions [ev_drought_hazard_teo22_1].
forest_restoration__drought__mixed_crop_.conditionality: The Tigray yield advantage was larger in the drier first year than in the following one, and it compares exclosures with open grazing, so it measures a downstream benefit to cropland rather than production on the restored land itself [ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_3]. The Ethiopian meta-analysis bundles exclosure and planting with bunds and terraces, the India and Afghanistan sheets bundle planting, regeneration and protection, and the WOCAT units are compiler ratings, not measurements, with the Afghanistan compiler rating drought impacts only slightly reduced [ev_soil_water_retention_meaza22_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_7460_2024_drought_impacts]. The modelled benefit is landscape-scale only and the source notes that most regional changes were not significant, so it does not speak to plot-scale restoration [ev_drought_hazard_teo22_1].

forest_restoration__drought_hazard.mechanism: WOCAT compilers report that assisted natural regeneration in Niger reduces drought impacts by improving vegetation cover and woody production, and that broadleaf plantations and assisted regeneration in India improved surface and subsurface hydrological functioning in the upper watershed; the Khost site in Afghanistan is also rated as reducing drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_2325_2017_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_5243_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_7460_2024_drought_impacts]. A regional climate model found reforestation reduced the probability of extremely dry months in 9 of 15 regions [ev_drought_hazard_teo22_1].
forest_restoration__drought_hazard.conditionality: The field evidence is compiler ratings without measured drought outcomes, and the model unit is a landscape-scale scenario in which most regional changes were not significant.

forest_restoration__fire__all.mechanism: The sub-practices disagree, so this row states conflicting evidence rather than a single effect. On the side of lower fire risk is protection and community forest management: villagers in India guard the forest from anthropogenic and wild fires, and greener cover with less flammable pine-needle build-up lowers the risk of burning, and a World Bank evaluation lists reduced incidence of fires among the environmental outcomes that participatory forest management projects reported where those outcomes were monitored [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_5243_2019_fire_risk, ev_fire_hazard_ieg13_1]. The passive regeneration row is split within itself: a Tanzanian enclosure is rated as reducing bush-fire hazard because of the enclosure, fire breaks and bylaws, while an Ethiopian area closure on degraded land is rated as slightly raising fire risk [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_1607_2014_fire_risk, ev_fire_hazard_wocat_1598_2014_fire_risk].
forest_restoration__fire__all.conditionality: What separates the sides in the evidence is active fire management: every unit that reports lower fire risk and gives a reason names protection measures (village guarding, fire breaks, bylaws), whereas the Ethiopian closure that rates fire risk higher describes no such measure and gives no reason [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_5243_2019_fire_risk, ev_fire_hazard_wocat_1607_2014_fire_risk, ev_fire_hazard_wocat_1598_2014_fire_risk]. Closing land to let forest recover should therefore not be assumed to reduce fire risk unless fire protection is part of the design. Apart from the World Bank evaluation, which gives a portfolio-level narrative without magnitudes and covers only projects that monitored the outcome [ev_fire_hazard_ieg13_1], all units are practitioner ratings. The effect is off-site for farmers: it applies to the restored forest and the landscape around it, not to their plots.

forest_restoration__flood__all.mechanism: In this evidence restored forest cover lowers flood peaks mainly at local scale and for smaller storms. Catchment models show it: in Slovakia's Hornad watershed a reforestation scenario cut a simulated flood peak from 84.8 to 74.9 m3/s and, for a 50% increase of forest, reduced peaks by about 24% on average in rain-duration tests, more for short storms than long ones [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_1, ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_3], and an afforestation simulation for Luxembourg's Alzette basin decreased the peak by 8% [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_5]. A systematic review found that flooding or peak flows decreased with forest cover expansion in 82% of the studies reporting them [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]. In a clear-cut Oregon basin, peak discharges recovered gradually as the basin revegetated, which the authors attribute to changes in evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. An FAO synthesis expects flash flooding to be reduced locally for frequent short, low-intensity storm events where soils are deep [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_7], and a global review states that afforestation in energy-limited environments will help to reduce flood risks [ev_flood_hazard_zhang17_1]. WOCAT compilers for area closures in Ethiopia, afforestation in Eritrea, Cabo Verde and Bosnia and Herzegovina, floodplain reafforestation in Tajikistan and a learning site in Afghanistan rate downstream flooding or flood impacts as reduced; an Ethiopian compiler notes that runoff from the watershed is highly reduced, and the Afghan compiler that riverbanks were revegetated with communities planting cuttings along banks and shorelines [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1072_2011_downstream_flooding, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1048_2011_downstream_flooding, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1330_2010_downstream_flooding, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1509_2011_flood_impacts, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_7460_2024_flood_impacts].
forest_restoration__flood__all.conditionality: What separates the benefit from the nulls is scale and storm size. The gains are local, modelled or small-storm results; the nulls are about large basins and floods on the plains. The FAO synthesis finds no evidence that reforesting watersheds reduces or prevents floods except at the very local scale of a few hundred hectares [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_5, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_6]. A Himalayan analysis concludes that reforestation will not likely have significant beneficial impact on local flooding, and certainly not on the hydrological character of the Ganges and Brahmaputra mainstreams [ev_flood_hazard_ives87_1], and a conference overview warns that reforestation in the mountains conceived as a palliative for the problems of the plains is likely to reap only disappointment [ev_flood_hazard_ivesmt87_1]. An FAO–CIFOR review concludes that massive programmes of forestation proclaimed as the answer to preventing floods simply will not do the job, although reforestation may have many other benefits [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_3], and a published comment argues that reforestation does not necessarily reduce flooding, for example if soil properties do not recover, river bed morphology does not change, and settlements, roads and drains remain unaltered [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_5]. These are expert positions and reviews rather than new measurements.
